blocks.x: No, I could never get that coat back. He kept that coat, it was a blue shirt and suit I had bought at Mark's Isaac and he never was giving my coat back. I guess look now, he could buy me a hundred coats right now. I want him to have a coat and a tie on, like the rest of us, you see. I used him on piano. He used to be some scared to work with him. He wouldn't have been for Harrison Braden, his brother-in-law, Barrett. He wouldn't have made that job, you

know? So he brought him on up. Let's start off at the beginning, if we can. Let's get your name down. My name, Abby Williams. That's your father? A-B-E-I-E. We'll get that straight. And what's your name? Paul Crawford. And mine is Dick Allen. Can we start at the very beginning of your life, when you were born and where?

Yeah, you want to start now. Born here in New Orleans, 1906 September 22nd. Raised in New Orleans. Raised in New Orleans. What's that? Right here. Down Philly Shandris Street. Which? Philly Shandris. Down the night war. That's what I was born at. Did you hear much music around the house, your family play around the house? Oh wow, I follow the, I like it. I follow the music and drums. Drums were really my, drum was really my, my praise. Sticking. Sticking. Sticking. Sticking. Sticking.
You were talking about how drums were your craved, huh?

Yeah, yeah, I loved it. I loved the drums. I used to go to the Lyrics Theater and they had this guy, you're a red happy drummer. And this was my seat in the show, right by him. He had more runs than anybody in the world. And this guy, his brother, I played with him, Lil Jim, he died, bass drummer, Black Benny. I used to follow the parades. He was playing with Papa Celestan. And I used to carry his bass drum. And when they had a job, a parade when I'd leave, and from Chris Kelly, he had Faso and Mila Barnes was playing with Faso as a drummer. And I used to bang on his drums. So finally my mother bought me a snare drum. Oh I had the touch and all, you know what I mean? So she bought me a snare drum and I waged around and got me a bass drum. And then I used to play for them. They had a lot of piano and drums in. Parties? Yeah, dances. Yeah, real, change things. That's what they really was using, piano and drums in the houses, you know what I mean? This was house parties, not a big dance. No, house parties. Piano and drums was using at that time. They would, you know. So then after finally, when I was making my career, I was going along with Joseph Thomas. Worked with him about for five years. And then after Joseph Thomas, well I commenced getting a lot of work myself, you see. Going around we had a good hustle for the band, you know what I mean? So therefore we had to split up. But that's me and Lawrence, Marrero, and George Lewis took in together, you see. Because I was in between time working in the WPA band. See, Said Frazier was my teacher. See I used to set set beside Said Frazier and George Riley and Ernest Chapania. After Ernest Chapania used to send me out on a lot of these jobs because he was a real street man. Ernest Chapania was, I know you're a talker. He was a real street man on the street. He was Celestine Head Man and the Brass Man. Because Chani Babi was his orchestra drummer. But he didn't like to play in the orchestra much? Who that? Trapania. No, no, no. He didn't care. Every time he had something he'd call on me and send me. No, he didn't care too much. I guess probably after he was getting old, you know, older and older, you see. Probably the time when I was doing the WPA time, you know.
How old do you figure he was? Much older than you, huh?
Who, Ernest Chapania? Oh yeah, Ernest Chapania was an old man.
About 20 years older than you? 30, 40?
No, I couldn't excimate on that. I couldn't excimate on that. I knew he was an older man than me. I was a youngster.
I don't know. Did you have any musicians in your family? Or did your mother sing or anything like that?

No, it wasn't. One was a, he was a guitar player. And that was Reverend Griffin's brother, Kenderman, you know, my mother. He was a guitar player. What was his name? Nah, I can't think of his name now. He did so long, man.

Was he down in the Ninth Ward? Huh? Yeah. He down in the Ninth Ward? Yeah, Ninth Ward, yeah. Did you know Ambrose and Henry Ford and those guys and Freddie Gould and all those guys down in the Ninth Ward? Yeah, yeah. Were they playing when you were young?

Freddie Gould and them? When you were a kid, yeah. Well they, I don't know if they, they didn't, they wasn't, you know what I mean? They come up way after in the time, you know what I mean? Playing, you know? They come up way after. But the old man was.
Who's that?
Yeah. They father. Yeah, he was playing. Man, them boys come up way behind, you know? Yeah, they come way after.
Who were some of the piano players around when you were coming up?

The piano players? This boy here, Noonie. Noonie Perez, who was a, Bauhaus piano player. Because I was playing with Son Wilson then, trumpet player and that was, he's a piano player. And they real tunk, you know what I mean? Yeah, I know. Real tunk, yeah, yeah. I know from, and Simon, Simon, Boynel San Diego, Black San Diego, Mitchell Frazier.
Was he any kind of Simon?
Yeah, his cousin. He was a hell-fired man too.
Simon Frazier and Mitchell Frazier.
Yeah. And Ellick Frazier, that was, all of them was piano players. And Lil' Dave made his first career with me, Dave Williams. Lil' Dave made his first career with me. You know? Oh yeah.
Well who was Son Wilson? I don't know how they know him.
Son Wilson, he's a trumpet player from the Third Ward.
Around the battlefield.
That's right, that's where he was at. Little bit of guy, he had nice cool black hair. Little bit of face.
Was he a star?
No, he was a, he was a Bauhaus. Yeah. Yeah, he played all Bauhaus music. See him and Clayton and them come up from around in that same
percentage. Who did Son Wilson have in his band?
He had, he had me, him, and this guy, Noonie, on piano. Let's see that was, uh, uh, she was. And he used to use Steve Anger, he used to use Steve Anger all the time.
Oh yeah.
On, on clarinet.
Oh yeah.
See?
Trombone?
No, clarinet.
He didn't have a trombone though?
No, no trombone. Only time if he'd get a big job or something like that, uh, he worked, uh, with Franky Dewson. He was a good man. Franky Dewson died.
Oh yeah, I heard plenty about him.
Yeah, he worked a lot of jobs with him. He was a good dunk man too.
What kind of numbers were they doing? Yeah.

They played all these, uh, like, uh, the three sixes. See, because there's a copy from Chris Kelly, you see, all of them used to go from the blues, you see, and Careless Love, which was Chris Kelly, he was the man, he was the king of blues, because that was number D. He futures, you understand what I mean? And they'd play, uh, like, Shake It and Break It, St. Louis blues, uh, uh, Dinah was very popular, you know, and, uh, had this in the three sixes, you know, real low-down blues, you know? Uh, uh, yeah.
Do you know the words to that? Uh, uh, the, uh, you know?

Uh, uh, uh, uh, I heard your, uh, heard your mammy on Christmas Day, heard your sister on Christmas Day, dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear And everybody would holler, you know? And they would just come along with the jazz,
real rules. That's what they call DMF. Same number, DMF. Well it had dirty words. It had all the dirty words about your mother.

Yeah, on a Christmas day, she was making babies on Christmas day. Put you on a pillow, if I miss you, I don't want them the most. And then play that number around 12 o'clock at night and after a while you're going to see somebody hit the floor, they all get drunk and then that's the time right here at the place of various, it's a church now. The new hall, the old teaching hall, the economy hall, where we left from Sunday, where they toured that church down. Yeah, I know. And at the Copper Raiders, which, what you call them, he promoted a lot of dances. And I read Toots and Trimble Paul and Plutzum. There was another piano player from back there too. Plutzum? Plutzum. Remember his humpback head, he used to be like that?
I never didn't know him.
He was humpback, red, and a little short neck like that. He used to play very hard. Plutzum.
I don't think I ever knew him. He probably played.

He was way back. He was the one from way back. He died. Yeah, Plutzum. He would tie him up with Simon and Mitchell Frazier and all them, and Elliott Frazier and all them boys played piano. What you know about that? And Simon always was a good man. Simon left the liquor kit. But Boynell and Mitchell was two stars. They worked together on the same piano. And they fit right together, huh?
That's right, right together. Well Mitchell must have been good if he
could play with Bernal. Oh yeah. Mitchell was great, man. Wonderful man.

Well how was Red Toots then? Red Toots, he was good. That's Washington, the guy that lives up in Shrewsbury. Yeah. Yeah, he's back in the union now. He just came back. He and Teddy Johnson just came back. Yeah. I got a little work together, I think. But anyhow, you were saying those guys would hit the floor?

Oh, when they did get high. I mean, at that time around twelve o'clock, they know the dance gonna break up about two o'clock, and everybody got drunk. And that's where they get to battle them up, Monkson. Man, you look there, somebody fighting start there, fighting. Somebody got another catch broad, you know, man, and shake around. And the floor walkers, at that time, we had a lot of bouncers around. And if they catch you cutting up too much, well they put you out, you know. Because that's why they didn't allow you, they didn't want you to come in without a coach, you know. Sometimes the catchers just get rugged and put you out. And then it would start a confusion, you understand? It would start a fight amongst them. And that, you heard of Talker Shottnake, that was Neely Hawking. He had the Imperial Jazz Band.
I can't remember him. What did he play? What happened?
Trumpet.
Shotneck.

Yeah, he had got shot in the neck one time. They would call him shot. Him and Howard and Sheik, Chris Kelly taught it them. But Sheik never had come out nowhere with them fellas. They all come out top trumpet players. And he just gave up, went out, and nearly Hawkins is his right name, or we called him Shotneck. He just went out and gave it up, you know, and after the time he got shot, standing looking at the parade. We used to have a lot of night parades. He was standing at the man Claiborne looking at the Bulls' parade and caught a straight bullet. Then he gave it up and he joined Churches, Deacon and the Churches down. But he was a fine trumpet band. He used to play in a brass band with Manuel Perez. And this cat had the Ricker band, he's in Chicago, New York somewhere, Charlie Remy. See he run that band, Charlie Remy. They all worked together, Kid Rene. Yeah they used to, they used to work there in Wood and Jewel.
Did you have another, you talk about those bouncers, did you have another guy called Foots, Papa Foots?
Yeah I remember Foots.
But what did he do?

Foots, all he did around, kind of a strong arm, you know. And just like you got these guys out in Boydman Street, you know what I mean, with like a humbuck store up there, he'd get there and he'd break it up like a referee or something like that. Well that's what he used to do.
Have a stick or something?
No, uh-uh. Nothing with his hands.
With his hands.
With his hands.
He must have been quite a man.
Yeah.
Were those big guys? Tall?
Yeah, big drafting guys.
Well you had to do some of that yourself too though, huh? You had to break up those fights yourself.
Oh yeah, yeah. I was on a detailed Saturday night, better than 500 people. Quiet as a mouse. Where was it? In the Desire Project.
That's a quiet relationship.
That's rough. They killed Trina the week before last.
Policeman?
No. Monks themselves. And them three murders was down there. Three murders in that project.
Well that little girl, sixteen years old. That was down in the Night Ward. That was down

in the Night Ward. Yeah, three kills. But I know everybody and it's just the way you don't go in brutalizing a person, you know what I mean? You don't go in brutalizing a person. But the night you'll be with them and handle them, they'll always listen. They know you the law. They know you got the law in your hands, and if they be bracing, you got the
opportunity to hold them, to put them on. You understand what I mean? You got the ups

of them. So a lot of them, before it was the teenagers, they say, I'm a teenager, but if they're seventeen-year-old, I mean if they're fourteen, fifteen-year-old, we put them in the home. Put them in the, the seventeen-year-old, we hit them. See, some of them brother. When you hit them, you arrest them. And then you put your statement against them. The Jews, the law requires us for not to hit them, not to hurt them. But they want us to do it. They tell us, you know, and the way we say before you, they don't want you to do it. They want us to do it. So the Jews say, if it had been me, I would have killed you. The Jews don't want us to hear nothing after you get up there and sign and make a statement against them. You understand? Then the Jews, he handle them. And you take a, George Babin, man, he's rough. But a lot of things I went around, keep from going to court, of course I go to court to prostitute, prostitute or die. I'm losing time, I don't get paid for it. You know? Only time I get paid when the city calls me out, they send me out on a job. Send me out on a job at the take-care place. Or they call me from the headquarters. Or break it in or something like that, and I go. And then I go ahead and make that twenty dollars.
You're an honorary deputy sheriff. Yeah. But before, what were you? I'm a special

officer too. You're a special officer. Yeah, I'm a special officer and the sheriff. Otherwise I'm hiring two different commissions. I can work in, you know what I mean, I can work in a different parish. See? You got that deputy sheriff first day of June,
1966. Yeah. So you just got that. Yeah, I just got that. And you, uh...
I just said, here I've been having this. I've been carrying this now for nine years. That's the city. Yeah, special officer. Uh-huh. Yeah, department of police. Uh-huh. See that?
That's a long term. Yeah. Yeah. Well, but you do get a little pay for that. It's not just

for that. But pay? Oh sure, I get paid. But not a steady pay? No, I don't get no steady pay. See I'm not on the payroll. I'm just an officer but I'm not, I'm what you call an auxiliary. If you hire me, I get paid from you. You pay me, or your company pays me. We want you here for every night. Now it's other big deals, I go on. You see, I don't have none of them yet, I got them on at the place. I got a lot of convicts, pays $300, $400, $500, $200, $150, bond breakers. Bond breakers, get them bond breakers and bring them in and you get money right off the bat. Soon we bring them in. You understand? Even if the city policeman, he knows them, well we all works together. If he knows them, he gets a little iron, he contacts you and you arrest him, or he gets a hold of him, he turns that arrest over to me. I might be getting $500 out of that deal. Well the city don't know nothing about that. When I get that $500, I put $250 on him. See? He ain't gonna get nothing but he's still eight hours paid. He might get a little iron, you know, for capping this guy, but us we got, they got all the ratings up there, how much they give them. They done broke bonds, you see? And we the men on the lookout, we got their photographs and everything, you see? We got their mug. See they passed their mugs down to them, so we can't miss them. So we just go along, probably just like we are, from one place to the other, riding. Just like we're going and checking a giant, you know? No uniform, you know, plain clothes, just check around, you got that picture, you got that mug, and you look around the giant and that's your man. And you cap him and handcuff him and bring him in. And that's where the braid at. Of course, you make nice money, you make some nice money, but you got to be smart to it, you got to be very, very hip to it. Remember that time? The guy made his trambone, and had his trambone. That was a firehouse. Well this captain over there, this captain, this is his property. This is his property. And Dick had been telling me they stole his trambone. So this bastard was something and he had it in an old sack. I said, well come on over, I'm going to buy the trambone, I'm going to get it, and called in on him. And damn we didn't come there and catch him in the captain with that damn trambone. He stole it out of his apartment, he was painting.
How long that been, Dick? I was helping him move. Must have been about 52, 53, huh? Yeah. Must have been that long. Yeah, I moved. Yeah, it was, yeah, well.
Yeah, he made the trambone. Then he comes to me to sell the trambone, and that's where he got tricked. Put him right in the trick bag, right over here in the firehouse.
I guess he's out of Angola now, wherever they put him, Paris Cruiser.
He's out. He sees me, man, he hits him. He's out now. Yeah.
Well we're getting all off of music. But what about Son Wilson? Did he play like anybody? Oh yeah. He played a job, a lot of parties. No, did he sound like anybody? Was he on Chris
Kelly's auto? Yeah, he was a real blues man, you know, a real tunk.
Something like Chris. Like Clayton. Like Clayton.

Yeah, Clayton. Clayton and Chris was real tunk man, you know what I mean? Howard too, he played a lot of tunk music too. You know? They got some of them guys trying to play, trying to imitate you know. They don't have the tone, the execution.
Well they don't sound right, those guys. They sound refined and classy and everything. Yeah. It makes a difference. When did you start playing in brass bands? We didn't get to that.

In brass bands? Oh, let's see. 1940. My first brass band job, when I played with Howard, I was playing with Howard. And then he and Lawrence, Lawrence Morell, and then they decided to form a brass band. Then I would play him with him. And in between time I'd play with Howard. You see? Then I was getting a lot of work myself, you see? And I never carried all the best Alvin Alcorn, Joe Phillip. I carried all the Hellfire fellas with me, you know? Because I had a lot of business in Sidney Diggs. You heard talk of Sidney Diggs. He had a Hellfire orchestra. Well I used to keep his band on the on crutches. I took one of his good men's buttons. I guess I probably just kept him on the Tato Point L. Oh yeah. I took him on the Tato Point L. Oh yeah. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. another orchestra, William and Ricard. You see? Well me and Ricard used to get, Ricard Lexi, we used to pick out all the best men. You see, because we paid them more. The scale was six dollars and they were making ten with us, ten and twelve. We paid them nothing under twelve dollars, they made double. Well you know that made Sidney had to call somebody else to put in his place. We used to call him White Roach. White Roach. Yeah. Said well Roach won't see me tonight. Well Joe Phillip liked whiskey and Poe Pointer, he liked to drink and he'd be up all day and he might have parades, I'd use him on parades. They never turned on because you had the ideal boys, you had the square deal boys, I was one of the tops in the square deal because I played all that work. You had the jolly boys, you had the Liberty Bells. Well me, George, William and all of them, we were fighting in between them with them bids, you see, I mean, and all of them was carrying two bands. Well they got so they wouldn't let one man run two-liter speed, you know. So we had a doggone good then because if we catch an own union man working on a job, that was it. All we do is just jump right on in there and collect that fees and then they'd bring them before the board. They was much more stricken and the scale wasn't paying what it was paying. But they had a lot of work though. It was much more work for brass bands. Oh yeah, brass bands. Boyd gave it Sunday. And they had orchestra work too, they had a lot of
appetizer on, started on trucks you know. And what about Mardi Gras? Did you play many of those

the carnival? Oh yeah, I worked those white parades. I worked the carnival club, I worked the Eleonora, the Eleonora club, worked for the Lions, and jumped you know from one year to the other because they all paid big prices you know. I worked for the Lions for about four years straight. When I was working over in the pad at Funk and Manders. Then they formed a marching club. Well that made me, by me working there on Sundays, me and Howard and them working on Sundays, we worked at Matt and Lee. That made me just take over for their parade. Then I had to find a way to get another band for them. Well they operated for about three years, I played for them about three years on the parade. .
I used to rehearse with a white fella, Paul Lane. Paul Lane? Yeah.
What did he play?
He was a guitar player and he had a family band, white.
And you used to go on rehearsals?

I used to rehearse with the next door neighbor. His sister played bass, played one of them bass. He played Dixieland music, you know. And the other fella they called Oscar, Oscar Pierce, he played piano.
It's all new names to me.
Yeah, the fella from way, way back.

Let's see, well this is already the third reel of Abby Williams. Not really. Not really. The first one didn't work. Hold on, there's so many people I want to ask you about and we're getting it all mixed up. After you finished playing these little parties, what kind of parties were they that you played with the piano players?
Well that was like, it was twenty-five cents to come in. Was it a fish fry or just for food?
No, no.
No, they had fish fry. We played the fish fry. But these was real house parties. You know? Long parties inside?
Inside, in the house.
In the house. No long parties. Piano, second room and third room. All the front is out. And that's where the thing went on at. I used to give them too.
Did they do that to make the rent ever? Eh? Did they ever do that so they could make the rent in different places?
No, well they'd get together and probably say it was like a little club. See? Sundu had his band then. He had, what's his name was Sundu's band? The Boozang Kings.
Oh yeah. Just kids, huh? Youngsters.
He started off on ukulele. That's what he started off on. Sundu.
Danny Barker. Danny Barker, yeah.
Eucalyte. And finally recently he went on and went on. When you come to find out he left town and went up the line, he used to come back and forward and he was up there doing good.
Back now? Huh? He's back now?
Yeah, he told me he's back to stay now. He lost his health.
No point in staying up there when you're healthy.
No, unless he's harmed me. It's like he told me, we played about two months ago at Chaddard Hospital. He told me, say, you know I never give up New Orleans, this is my home.
You've got a few projects, huh? Playing at charity and different places.
Yeah I played one not long ago with Paul Bourne. I've got another one coming up now. At the charity?
Yeah, I've got another one coming up.
I've got one of my own, you know, coming up. That's good.
Well after you played those little two piece jobs, who did you get with then?
You mean who did I went with?
Yeah, what band did you go with then?
Went with then, I went with Joseph Thomas.
You said something about picnics too, you played picnics.
Yeah, well we played, we broke the record in picnics. We had more picnics than any band in the city of New Orleans.
Well what happens at a picnic like that? Is it out of doors or indoors?

No, it's something in the pavilion. Out on the pavilion they got halls, you know. And down at that time there wasn't no buses, there was trucks. You know, they'd have trucks and clubs and Thomas was working for Solara then. And Solara gave one of the biggest picnics, you know. And then we was connected with the K&B, Catherine Bestra's employees. And there used to be what and what, but they never was on the same day.
And would they go out in the country?

Yeah, go out in the country, go out to La Plaste, maybe they might go to, go to Arlington, across the river, you know. They went to different places, they never went to the same place. They went to La Vida Spring, Pas Christiane, they went to different places. Go down to Sebastopol.
What would they do at one of those, you know, before I ever came to town?

Well, all they did, you pay your fare, say the tickets might be a dollar round trip. That dollar round trip, it admits you in the hall. And if you didn't have a ticket, it was then at that door when they get there with the van and things, you'd have to pay fifty cents to come in if you didn't sneak in. Because a lot of people had their own cars, you know, automobiles, go along and they call. And then they sell their refreshments and stuff. Some people bring their refreshments to get out on the lawn, you know, in the yard, different things. Some of them get up on the levee banks. And then the rest of them will be up in there dancing.
What kind of refreshments would they have?
Oh, they'd have all kinds of, eat sandwiches, you know, and beer, whiskey. Wine selling just like a drink.
Yeah, I see. You understand?
Yeah, they sell it, they come.
You could bring your own basket if you wanted.
Yeah, yeah, most of them bring their baskets. Yeah, they bring their baskets.
Well, who was in that, that was Cornbread's band, right? Who was that?

Yeah, Joseph Thomas. Who was in the band? We used a fella called Julius, Julius on banjo, damn good banjo, sort of Jamaica bar. Henry Ricksnell, he's a male carter. He was a good man. He was the one who made Rene, Kid Rene, look like 15 cents. When this number, we got this number before them, music go round and round, because he was a smart fella. He was just like Blue. Of course he's a better man than Blue because anything he wanted, he could read it, you know, hold his up on. But he had a double of a head, you know, on his body, Henry Ricksnell. He's a male carter now. He went to the Army, you know. And we had that number when music go round and round, and that number sold.
Oh, I know.

That number sold. We put nine hundred, nine hundred people at the Gypsy Tea Room. We played there. We packed them in nine hundred that night. Paul Barber ain't coming behind the next night. He had about four hundred people. We went in on a Saturday night, Paul come in on a Sunday night.
That was Rick Snell was a trumpet player.
Yeah, Henry Rick Snell.
That's funny, I never heard of him. But he, and let's see, did you have a bass player, a trombone player?
A bass player died. P.T. I don't know him. He was a big fellow, he was a painter, tall, very fat.
P.T.
P.T. P.T.
That was his last name? Yeah. I heard of Joe P.T. and Buddy P.T. and T.E.T. Roussone.
P.T. And trombone or saxophone? He was a bass player. Did you have a trombone?
Who did I? In that band with Coyne Brad? Oh, sometime, Eddie Summers, that's his, I used to use Eddie Summers. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Did you ever use a piano?

Oh, sometime, Eddie Summers, that's his, I used to use Eddie Summers. You ever use a piano? Piano, yeah. We use a piano. Now this boy, I see this boy all the time and I can't think of his name. He's old. Joe Lewis. He's a Dixieland fool.
I don't know Joe Lewis. I know Walter Lewis. Little bit of Brownskins, brother. Stay back on Pearl Street. Oh, I don't know where he lives. It might be the same guy that might
have two names. He drinks a whole lot. That's him. That was his regular piano. That was Thomas' regular piano player. We called him Joe Lewis, all in the
history of the life. Joe Lewis was a popular name about that time.

Yeah. Played plenty of piano, Dixieland man. He figured he plays a lot of jobs now that he figured he'd come back in the union. Oh, he'd play on any kind of old broken piano. He'd put you in mind of Mitchell Fridge in there. Played all over the Bad Keys. Doesn't worry, man. No. Well, anyway. And sometimes they used to use
little Sammy Hopton. Mm-hmm. But I hardly see him anymore.

He's interesting. I saw him about a monocle. You see what is happening now, that union is kind of breaking up some of them fellas now. He's teaching. Leonard Eberidge. Yeah, well, I've seen him. See, he used to give me permission to use him. Otherwise, we used to be real lean on the schools. We gave the school children a lot of breaks. And sometimes in the summer time, in the carnival time, I had to use very few men's in the city. I'd send home. And I'd get this boy, Emory, Big Emory, first of the hundred brothers. He was up there in college. How many times did he get? Yeah, he'd bring, because he was going to make ten or fifteen, twenty dollars, you know, for himself. And boy, he'd bring them down. He'd bring them down. He'd bring them down. He'd get them down. And then when I used to pay off, I'd pay him off. Then And then when I used to pay off, I'd pay him off. Then he'd pay them off. But I had them hired for thirty-five dollars, thirty-five dollars a man. Poor Bob was up there broke and saw me, they had a dime in their pocket. They was glad to get on there for fifteen or twenty dollars. To get back on the campus, we'd have something to go back on the campus with.
You played with a lot of brass bands, I remember through the years from time to time. Different ones like the Young Tuxedo, you were with them pretty regular for a while.
I played with Tuxedo.

Oh yeah, I got work for them.
Well I mean how do you do that?

Well you see, you know fellas in the club. Then you know something is going on. Then you get next to the chairman and he said bring the bid in, bring your bid in, he'd tell you the time, you know, the hours. Then you'd get in there and you'd beat the other guy, the other guy, well they wouldn't even recognize the other fella, they want you. And that's where you would, that's where you would, I'd get the wood. You take like the Square Deal, I had the Square Deal boys sold up. They had a wonderful club there. And T. Shan died. Remember Vic T. Shan?

Oh.

Yeah man, he played plenty bass drum. He could take off where anybody left off at.

Uh-huh.

Uh-huh.

You understand? I see. There was so much to do with the second line and on, and then we used to parade just like the, like the veteran. And I was a member of the young veteran. Yeah, they are.
At this block, the next block, he dies right there and he dies.
His nephew and them live across the street over there.

Around St. Thomas or Russo somewhere around there. Yeah. How long did you have to march for them? You walked for them all. You get your band up there for seven o'clock in the morning. You're up there for seven. Little after seven they blew the whistle. They're on a hike.

I don't think they start until eight now. They're corner club now starts at eight. But the buzzers and all them, the lines, they all start at seven o'clock. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They lay up there by the park. Yeah. They got their long heights. They're on a hike.
I don't think they start until 8 now.
They're a carnival club now starts at 8. But the buzzers and all them, the lions, they all start at 7 o'clock.
Yeah, they're out there by the park.
Yeah, they got a long hike.
And they got more to drink, shouldn't they? Oh yeah. Got more stocks to make, I guess. All those ballrooms.
But you see, I put them down because the buzzers now, the buzzers in the corner club is the easiest job up there now.
Why?
They go one way.
They get back on the bar.

Yeah, you walk down and then you ride up. You ride up and then you finish up in the territory. So, Anderson said he think, that's until they come up with that hundred dollars. Anderson said he think he gonna give the, I have to call them up. Because they're the only one who got that hard job. The lions. The lions, yeah. Yeah. You see what then happened, a lot of young fellas, them youngsters, is taking the old man's place, the one who's died or the others in the club. And they taking over the children. And they can do that damn walking, man. Man, they skipping up all day long. You see? It don't move them. It don't even move them. You know?
Well, they must be newer. Well, the buzzers I know are the oldest. Huh? The buzzers are the oldest. I know they've been there longer than anybody.
Yeah, the buzzers have been there the longest.

Yeah.
This school down... In St. Bernard?

Yeah, we got that.

Paul Barnes, yeah.

Mm-hmm.
See?

Yeah.

Well, Rickard was playing bass then or trumpet? Rickard was playing trumpet. And you had two trumpets, huh?
When? When... Well, you said you had another trumpet who was in the local. You can't think of his name. Well... A different time.
